marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q001.takeaway: The intertrochanteric line is the anterior ridge joining the greater and lesser trochanters at the proximal femur.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q001.displayText:
The intertrochanteric line is the anterior ridge joining the greater and lesser trochanters at the proximal femur.

The structure related to the anterior surface of the proximal femur is the intertrochanteric line, present at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur (head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters; intertrochanteric line anteriorly and intertrochanteric crest posteriorly), shaft (linea aspera on the posterior surface, gluteal tuberosity, pectineal line), and distal femur (medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa and patellar surface).

Spiral fractures of long bones such as the femur or humerus in a child suggest an external twisting force and are highly suspicious for non-accidental trauma; the source calls the probable diagnosis battered baby syndrome.
emphasis: The intertrochanteric line is the anterior ridge joining the greater and lesser trochanters at the proximal femur

rationales.a: Linea aspera is the prominent longitudinal ridge on the posterior femoral shaft, not the anterior proximal landmark.
rationales.b: The pectineal line lies proximally on the posterior shaft and is not on the anterior intertrochanteric region.
rationales.d: The intertrochanteric crest is the posterior ridge between the trochanters; the anterior ridge is the intertrochanteric line.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q002.takeaway: The normal femoral neck–shaft angle is about 125°; larger angles are coxa valga and smaller angles coxa vara.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q002.displayText:
The normal femoral neck–shaft angle is about 125°; larger angles are coxa valga and smaller angles coxa vara.

The normal angle of the neck of the femur to the shaft is approximately 125°. This is the neck-shaft angle or angle of inclination.

This facilitates movement at the hip joint. An angle greater than 135° is coxa valga, while an angle less than 120° is coxa vara.
emphasis: The normal femoral neck–shaft angle is about 125°; larger angles are coxa valga and smaller angles coxa vara

rationales.a: 105° is below the usual adult neck-shaft angle and is in the coxa-vara direction.
rationales.c: 135° is above the typical angle and approaches coxa valga rather than the normal value.
rationales.d: 115° is below the usual approximate 125° adult angle.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q003.takeaway: The linea aspera is a posterior femoral ridge; it gives attachment to adductor longus and other thigh muscles/septa.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q003.displayText:
The linea aspera is a posterior femoral ridge; it gives attachment to adductor longus and other thigh muscles/septa.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). The linea aspera of the femur gives attachment to adductor longus, the intermuscular septa and the short head of biceps femoris.

Linea aspera is a roughened ridge on the posterior surface of the femoral shaft and has medial and lateral edges. Proximally the medial edge continues as the spiral line and the lateral edge as the gluteal tuberosity. Distally the medial border continues as the medial supracondylar line and the lateral border as the lateral supracondylar line; the surface between the supracondylar lines is the popliteal surface.
emphasis: The linea aspera is a posterior femoral ridge; it gives attachment to adductor longus and other thigh muscles/septa

rationales.a: The linea aspera lies on the posterior, not anterior, shaft of the femur.
rationales.b: The long head of biceps femoris arises from the ischial tuberosity; the short head arises from the linea aspera.
rationales.c: The lateral edge continues proximally as the gluteal tuberosity, while the medial edge continues as the spiral line.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q004.takeaway: The medial circumflex femoral artery is the principal adult supply to the femoral head through retinacular branches.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q004.displayText:
The medial circumflex femoral artery is the principal adult supply to the femoral head through retinacular branches.

The arterial supply to the femoral head is mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery.

The blood supply is derived from an arterial ring (trochanteric anastomosis) around the femoral neck formed by the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, branches of profunda femoris, with minor contributions from superior and inferior gluteal vessels.

In the fetus and early postnatal period the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries contribute equally; later the lateral circumflex contribution diminishes and supply is mainly from two major arteries of the medial circumflex femoral artery.

A small acetabular branch of the obturator artery reaches the femoral head through the ligament of the head of femur, but is a minor source.
emphasis: The medial circumflex femoral artery is the principal adult supply to the femoral head through retinacular branches

rationales.a: Lateral epiphyseal vessels are retinacular branches supplying the head and usually arise from the medial circumflex femoral artery; the keyed option names the principal parent source.
rationales.c: The artery in the ligament of the head is usually a small contribution after childhood and is insufficient as the principal adult supply.
rationales.d: The lateral circumflex contributes to the trochanteric anastomosis but is not the principal adult retinacular supply to the head.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q005.takeaway: The nutrient artery to the femoral shaft usually arises from the second perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q005.displayText:
The nutrient artery to the femoral shaft usually arises from the second perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery.

The second perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery is the nutrient artery to the femur.
emphasis: The nutrient artery to the femoral shaft usually arises from the second perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery

rationales.a: The femoral artery is the parent vessel for profunda femoris but the source identifies the second perforator as the nutrient-artery source.
rationales.b: The lateral circumflex femoral artery supplies surrounding muscles and contributes to anastomoses, not the usual femoral nutrient artery.
rationales.c: The medial circumflex femoral artery chiefly supplies the hip/head region and is not the typical shaft nutrient vessel.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q006.takeaway: The distal femoral secondary ossification center appears near term, around the ninth intrauterine month.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q006.displayText:
The distal femoral secondary ossification center appears near term, around the ninth intrauterine month.

The secondary ossification centre at the distal end of the femur appears in the ninth month (full-term) of intrauterine life and forms the condyles and epicondyles.

The femur ossifies from one primary and four secondary centres. The primary centre appears in the midshaft in the seventh week of prenatal life. Secondary centres appear at the distal end in the ninth month of intrauterine life, the head at six months after birth, the greater trochanter in the fourth year and the lesser trochanter between the twelfth and fourteenth years.
emphasis: The distal femoral secondary ossification center appears near term, around the ninth intrauterine month

rationales.a: The femoral-head center appears about six months after birth, later than the distal femoral center.
rationales.b: The greater trochanter center appears in early childhood, not by term.
rationales.c: The lesser trochanter center appears in adolescence, not during fetal development.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q007.takeaway: The upper end of the femur has three secondary centers: head, greater trochanter and lesser trochanter.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q007.displayText:
The upper end of the femur has three secondary centers: head, greater trochanter and lesser trochanter.

The upper end of the femur ossifies from three ossification centers: the head (appears at 6 months after birth), greater trochanter (4th year), and lesser trochanter (12–14 years).
emphasis: The upper end of the femur has three secondary centers: head, greater trochanter and lesser trochanter

rationales.a: One center would omit the separate head and trochanteric centers.
rationales.b: Two centers would omit one of the three distinct proximal secondary centers.
rationales.d: Four overcounts the femoral upper-end centers; the shaft primary center is not part of the upper end.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q008.takeaway: The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the femoral patellar surface.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q008.displayText:
The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the femoral patellar surface.

The patella is a sesamoid bone formed within the tendon of the quadriceps femoris. It is triangular and lies in the patellofemoral groove; the inferior apex gives attachment to the patellar ligament and the superior base gives attachment to quadriceps femoris.

Its convex anterior surface is perforated by numerous nutrient vessels and separated from the skin by a prepatellar bursa. The posterior surface has an oval articular area crossed by a smooth vertical ridge that fits the intercondylar groove; the ridge divides the articular surface into medial and lateral facets that articulate with the corresponding femoral condyles.

Important sesamoid bones listed by the source: patella in quadriceps femoris (largest sesamoid); pisiform in flexor carpi ulnaris; fabella in the lateral head of gastrocnemius; two sesamoids at the first metacarpal within flexor pollicis brevis/adductor pollicis tendons; and two at the first metatarsophalangeal articulation within the double tendon of flexor hallucis brevis.
emphasis: The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the femoral patellar surface

rationales.a: Flat bones are broad plates such as scapula; the patella develops within a tendon.
rationales.b: Pneumatic bones contain air spaces, a feature not present in the patella.
rationales.d: Irregular bones have complex shapes such as vertebrae; the patella is classified by its tendon-embedded development.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q009.takeaway: The tibial tuberosity forms the inferior apex of the triangular area on the anterior proximal tibia.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q009.displayText:
The tibial tuberosity forms the inferior apex of the triangular area on the anterior proximal tibia.

The apex of the tibial triangular area is formed by the tibial tuberosity.

The tibial triangular area lies in front of the anterior condylar surface. Its apex is directed downward and is formed by the tibial tuberosity; its base is continuous with the anterior condylar surfaces of the tibia.

The tibial tuberosity gives attachment to the patellar ligament and has a distal rough and proximal smooth region. The distal region is palpable and separated from skin by the infrapatellar bursa.
emphasis: The tibial tuberosity forms the inferior apex of the triangular area on the anterior proximal tibia

rationales.a: Epicondyles are projections associated with distal long bones and do not form this anterior tibial landmark.
rationales.b: The tibial crest continues inferiorly along the shaft, while the triangular area's pointed apex is the tuberosity.
rationales.d: The malleolus is a distal ankle projection, not the proximal triangular-area apex.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q010.takeaway: The tibial shaft primary ossification center appears at about the seventh week of intrauterine life.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q010.displayText:
The tibial shaft primary ossification center appears at about the seventh week of intrauterine life.

The primary ossification center of the tibia appears at the 7th week of intrauterine life.

The tibia ossifies from three centers: one primary centre in the shaft and two secondary centres, one at each epiphysis. The upper-end centre is usually present at birth and fuses with the shaft at about 16 years in females and 18 years in males. The lower-end centre appears early in the first year and fuses with the shaft at about 15 years in females and 17 years in males.
emphasis: The tibial shaft primary ossification center appears at about the seventh week of intrauterine life

rationales.a: The third week is too early for the tibial primary ossification center.
rationales.b: The fifth week precedes the source's approximate week-seven appearance.
rationales.d: The ninth week is later than the usual seventh-week appearance stated in the source.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q011.takeaway: Biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula, along with the fibular collateral ligament.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q011.displayText:
Biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula, along with the fibular collateral ligament.

The bone depicted is the fibula. Biceps femoris is attached to its head.

Important relations/attachments: fibular collateral ligament and biceps femoris attach to the head; the common peroneal nerve can be rolled against the neck. The shaft has three surfaces related to leg muscles: lateral surface to fibular muscles, anteromedial surface to extensors, and posterior surface to flexor muscles.
emphasis: Biceps femoris inserts on the head of the fibula, along with the fibular collateral ligament

rationales.a: The lateral meniscus attaches to the tibial plateau and is not the fibular-head attachment shown.
rationales.b: Popliteus arises from the lateral femoral condyle and inserts on posterior tibia, not the fibular head.
rationales.d: The posterior cruciate ligament attaches to the intercondylar areas of femur and tibia, not the fibular head.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q012.takeaway: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the fibular neck, making this site vulnerable to injury and foot drop.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q012.displayText:
The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the fibular neck, making this site vulnerable to injury and foot drop.

The likely fracture is at the neck of the fibula, which is closely related to the common peroneal nerve; injury causes foot drop.

Clinical considerations: the fibula does not transmit body weight and is a common source of bone graft; the lateral malleolus and its attached ligaments are important for ankle stability; the common peroneal nerve can be rolled against the fibular neck and is commonly injured; in the first stage of Pott's fracture the lower end of the fibula is fractured spirally.
emphasis: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the fibular neck, making this site vulnerable to injury and foot drop

rationales.a: A tibial-shaft fracture is not adjacent to the common peroneal nerve's superficial course at the fibular neck.
rationales.b: The fibular shaft lies distal to the nerve's vulnerable winding point at the neck.
rationales.d: The tibial tuberosity is anterior and proximal, not the site where the common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibula.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q013.takeaway: The fibula has three ossification centers: one primary shaft center and secondary centers at proximal and distal ends.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q013.displayText:
The fibula has three ossification centers: one primary shaft center and secondary centers at proximal and distal ends.

The fibula ossifies from three ossification centres: one primary centre in the shaft and two secondary centres at the extremities.

Ossification in the shaft begins at the 8th week of intrauterine life. The distal end appears in the first year and unites with the shaft by about 15 years in females and 17 years in males. The proximal end appears at 3–4 years and unites with the shaft at around 17 years in females and 19 years in males.
emphasis: The fibula has three ossification centers: one primary shaft center and secondary centers at proximal and distal ends

rationales.a: Two centers would omit either the primary shaft or one of the two epiphyseal centers.
rationales.c: Four centers overcounts the usual shaft-plus-two-ends pattern.
rationales.d: Five centers is not the standard count for fibular ossification.

marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q014.takeaway: The navicular lies between the head of the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally.
marrow__ANAT_CH54_Q014.displayText:
The navicular lies between the head of the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally.

The navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

There are seven tarsal bones in the proximal half of the foot. The proximal row is the talus and calcaneum. The distal row from medial to lateral contains the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms and cuboid. Medially, the navicular lies between the talar head and the cuneiforms.
emphasis: The navicular lies between the head of the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally

rationales.a: The calcaneus lies posterior/inferior to the talus, not between the talar head and cuneiforms.
rationales.b: The cuboid lies lateral to the navicular and articulates with the calcaneus and lateral metatarsals.
rationales.d: Metatarsals lie distal to the tarsal bones and do not intervene between talus and cuneiforms.
